passages.t: ‘May God be gracious to us and bless us’, so that all nations may know
passages.happening:
This short psalm is a blessing that opens outward. “May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us” (verse 1). Why? So “that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations” (verse 2).

A refrain comes twice. “Let the peoples praise You, O God; let all the peoples praise You” (verses 3 and 5). Between them, the reason: “Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for You judge the peoples justly and lead the nations of the earth” (verse 4).

Then a harvest. “The earth has yielded its harvest; God, our God, blesses us” (verse 6). And the last line says it all again. “God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The first line would ring a bell. It echoes the blessing God gave the priests to speak over Israel: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24-25). Every Israelite heard those words in worship. The psalm takes them and turns ‘you’ into ‘us’, as the people pray them back.

A shining face meant favour, like a king smiling on someone who came before him. Psalm 13 felt the opposite: a hidden face.

Verse 6 points to a harvest, so the psalm may have been sung at a harvest feast. The Hebrew can also be read as a prayer for a harvest still to come.

The surprise is the purpose. The blessing is not only for Israel to enjoy. It is so that the nations will see and come to know God. That goes back to God's first promise to Abraham: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).
passages.later:
When old Simeon held the baby Jesus in the temple, he praised God for a salvation prepared “in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel” (Luke 2:31-32).

Isaiah heard God say to his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). And Revelation sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9).
passages.asks:
This psalm asks why you want God's blessing. For your own comfort? Or so that others will see what God is like?

Verse 7 links the two: ‘God blesses us, that all the ends of the earth shall fear Him.’ Blessing is meant to be passed on. Who around you could see God's kindness through the good things he has given you?
